routes.description: Establish that Bignon's experience, providentially interpreted coincidences, and supporting intellectual and historical considerations can jointly provide rational support for specifically Christian belief without compelling every observer.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the experiential pattern is rationally relevant under a comparative explanation, rival experiences do not neutralize it, and independent considerations can support its Christian interpretation at the modest standard of personal rational justification.

motionBridge.description: Show that the conversion experience and supporting considerations jointly make Christian belief rationally supportable despite naturalist and rival-religion alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Explain why the personally salient convergence of experiences and coincidences is more expected under providence than under an unaided naturalistic account.
Connect experience with intellectual considerations so the case supplies rational justification without requiring coercive or universally compelling proof.
Provide a principled way to distinguish the Christian interpretation from incompatible religious experiences through comparative intellectual and historical considerations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for why providential guidance in one conversion need not imply equivalent guidance or conversion opportunities for every person.
Clarify how surviving early Christian materials can aid access to historical claims without treating their abundance alone as proof of those claims.

routes.description: Establish that reverse conversions, culturally variable experiences, ordinary coincidence, and competing intellectual considerations remove any distinctive evidential advantage claimed for Bignon's Christian interpretation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic explanations adequately predict conversion patterns, rival experiences resist a uniquely Christian reading, and the proposed intellectual or historical adjudicators do not restore a clear evidential advantage.

motionBridge.description: Show that rival experiences and naturalistic explanations undercut the claimed evidential force of Bignon's experience for specifically Christian belief.

centralBridges.description: Explain how large populations, ordinary coincidence, and culturally familiar narratives can generate apparently coordinated conversion stories without providential causation.
Show how culturally diverse and directionally opposed religious experiences weaken an inference from personal experience to Christianity in particular.
Establish that philosophical and historical considerations remain contested and do not plainly break the symmetry between Christian, rival-religious, and naturalist interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether selective providential intervention fits the persistence of reasonable nonbelief and the uneven distribution of conversion experiences.
Distinguish evidential quality from documentary quantity by considering how institutional dominance and preservation affect the surviving record.

sections.title: Providential pattern or natural coincidence
sections.rationale: This section addresses the primary explanatory clash over whether the conversion story's coordinated and personally salient events favor divine providence or are expected among many lives shaped by ordinary coincidence and familiar narratives.

sections.title: Personal justification and the cumulative case
sections.rationale: This section fixes the relevant epistemic burden and examines how experience, philosophical argument, and background considerations may combine to support belief without forcing rational convergence or excluding reasonable disagreement.

sections.title: Rival religious experiences and Christian specificity
sections.rationale: This section tests whether culturally diverse experiences, reverse conversions, and disputed exceptions neutralize specifically Christian support, or whether different experiences can be compared without dismissing all experiential evidence.

sections.title: Historical and intellectual adjudication
sections.rationale: This section considers whether historical sources and broader intellectual arguments can adjudicate between Christianity and rival interpretations when experiential claims appear balanced, including the significance and limits of the surviving documentary record.

sections.title: Selective providence and persistent nonbelief
sections.rationale: This section examines whether a providential account of one person's conversion can accommodate uneven divine guidance, persistent reasonable nonbelief, and competing considerations concerning hiddenness without undermining the proposed explanation.
